scope: Original manuscript figure PDFs rendered without altering their scientific content.

figures.caption: The figure displays exact coefficient matrices for $d=2$, $m=3$. The combined row support of two seeds has rank three. The bar heights record algebraic orbit dimensions and should not be read as probabilities of unitary state preparation.
figures.alt: Three exact seed examples with orbit dimensions two, four, and six.
figures.description: The left panel lists coefficient matrices C1, C2, and C3. The bar chart gives orbit dimension two for C1, four for C2, and six for C2 together with C3, reaching the dashed full-space level. These heights are algebraic dimensions, not probabilities.

figures.caption: This rational model uses two coordinates to illustrate block inversion. Both the eliminated block and the full operator are invertible, and the plotted values are exact fractions. The example shows why direct compression and resolvent elimination give different results.
figures.alt: Compressed inversion differs from exact Schur elimination in a two-coordinate rational model.
figures.description: The displayed matrix has rows (2, 1) and (1, 3). Inverting the compressed entry gives one half. The Schur complement is five thirds, whose inverse is three fifths, equal to the retained entry of the full inverse. The three bars compare these exact fractions.

figures.caption: The figure shows exact weights for one supported code state. The normalized map preserves trace one, while the unnormalized positive map has output trace four. The illustration records this finite scaling distinction and does not assert a general recovery construction.
figures.alt: Normalized and unnormalized maps have output traces one and four.
figures.description: Two stacked bars separate identity and Z contributions. The normalized channel has weights three quarters and one quarter, totaling one. The unnormalized positive map has contributions three and one, totaling four. Equal relative weights do not fix total normalization.

figures.caption: The diagram shows the quantum realization of the common sequence of operators in the seed calculus. The same finite packet language describes states, gates, Hamiltonians, channels, geometric projectors, and effective dynamics.
figures.alt: The quantum seed calculus shown as a sequence of seven operator stages.
figures.description: Seven nodes are connected from left to right: seed, gates, project, transfer, refine, constrain, and reconstruct. The diagram organizes the finite operator language used across the chapter; it is not an experimental process diagram.

figures.caption: The eight computational packets of three qubits refine the two total-parity packets exactly.
figures.alt: Three-qubit computational addresses refine the even and odd parity packets.
figures.description: Two coarse nodes, even and odd parity, connect to the eight three-bit addresses. Each address belongs to the parity determined by its number of one bits. The links show refinement into computational packets while retaining the total parity grouping.

figures.caption: The Bell state generated from the seed $\ket{00}$.
figures.alt: Bell-state coordinate probabilities are one half at 00 and 11.
figures.description: The bar chart has four computational addresses: 00, 01, 10, and 11. The bars at 00 and 11 have height one half; the other two have height zero. This is the displayed Bell state prepared from the 00 seed.

figures.caption: Circuit reconstruction as a sum over packet paths.
figures.alt: Packet paths through the seed, Hadamard, and controlled-NOT stages.
figures.description: The horizontal axis shows seed, H, and CNOT stages. Each stage has even and odd packet nodes, with colored links indicating possible transfers between them. Summing the path contributions reconstructs the circuit action.

figures.caption: The Hamiltonian becomes exactly block diagonal when the even and odd basis vectors are grouped.
figures.alt: A two-qubit Hamiltonian heatmap grouped by even and odd parity.
figures.description: The basis is ordered 00, 11, 01, 10, so the even addresses come first. Nonzero matrix entries lie in the two diagonal parity blocks. Both off-diagonal blocks are zero, displaying parity-preserving transfer.

figures.caption: A perturbation that breaks parity creates nonzero transfer between the packets. The measured leakage remains below the commutator bound.
figures.alt: Measured parity leakage stays below the plotted commutator bound.
figures.description: The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is norm. The measured leakage curve rises below the straight commutator-bound curve throughout the plotted interval. This figure illustrates the retained finite perturbation experiment.

figures.caption: The equation in the moving frame holds to numerical precision only when the connection term is retained.
figures.alt: Moving-frame equation residuals with and without the connection term.
figures.description: Two bars use a logarithmic residual axis. Retaining the connection gives a residual near numerical precision; omitting it gives a much larger residual. The comparison isolates the connection term in the moving-coordinate equation.

figures.caption: The curvature of the Bloch projector, evaluated by finite differences, is compared with the exact density $\frac12\sin\theta$.
figures.alt: Finite-difference Bloch curvature agrees with the half-sine density.
figures.description: The plot compares the finite-difference curvature and the exact one-half sine-of-theta curve over the displayed polar-angle interval. Both rise to a central peak and fall to zero at the endpoints, with the curves visually coincident at this scale.

figures.caption: Amplitude damping transfers population from the excited packet to the ground packet while preserving trace and positivity.
figures.alt: Amplitude damping gives a diagonal mixture of ground and excited populations.
figures.description: A two-by-two density-matrix heatmap shows positive entries on the diagonal and zero off-diagonal entries for the displayed excited-state input. The ground population receives the damping contribution while the excited population retains the remainder.

figures.caption: The four orthogonal syndrome packets of the three-qubit bit-flip code. Each packet identifies one correctable error without resolving the encoded logical state.
figures.alt: Four syndrome projectors each select a pair of three-qubit addresses.
figures.description: Rows represent no flip and a flip of each of the three qubits. Columns list the eight computational addresses. Each row has two selected cells: 000 and 111; 100 and 011; 010 and 101; or 001 and 110. The row identifies an error without distinguishing the logical basis states inside it.

figures.caption: Exact Feshbach reduction versus bare truncation.
figures.alt: Exact Feshbach reduction has far smaller resolvent error than bare truncation.
figures.description: A logarithmic bar chart compares projected resolvent error. The exact Feshbach bar is near numerical precision, while the bare-truncation bar is substantially larger. The comparison retains the influence of the eliminated coordinates in one finite example.

figures.caption: Norms of packet Green-function blocks.
figures.alt: Norms of four packet-resolved Green-function blocks.
figures.description: A two-by-two heatmap places source parity on columns and target parity on rows. The two diagonal blocks have positive displayed norms; the off-diagonal blocks are zero in this example. The color scale represents block Frobenius norms.

figures.caption: The diagram organizes a conjectural nested packet tower for quantum geometry. It does not provide a numerical reconstruction of physical spacetime.
figures.alt: A conjectural refinement tree for quantum-spacetime packet sectors.
figures.description: Colored nodes and connecting branches show sectors subdividing through successive refinement levels. The horizontal axis is refinement level and the vertical axis is conceptual sector. The diagram organizes a proposed tower and does not reconstruct physical spacetime.

figures.caption: Positive spectrum of the Euclidean transfer operator.
figures.alt: The displayed Euclidean transfer eigenvalues are positive.
figures.description: Transfer eigenvalues are plotted by ordered mode on a logarithmic vertical axis. The points descend while remaining positive. The plot records the finite Euclidean transfer spectrum used in the manuscript.

figures.caption: Ground-state volume packet in the controlled toy model.
figures.alt: A localized ground-state volume distribution in a finite toy model.
figures.description: The horizontal axis is discrete spatial volume and the vertical axis is ground-state probability. A narrow peak appears around the center of the displayed volume range, with small tails toward both ends. Its interpretation is restricted to the controlled toy model.

figures.caption: The figure shows the finite Euclidean kernel for volume transfer. Positivity and semigroup composition hold exactly in the finite model. Its gravitational interpretation remains provisional.
figures.alt: A finite volume-transfer kernel concentrated near its diagonal.
figures.description: A heatmap uses source volume on columns and target volume on rows. The largest entries follow a diagonal band and decrease away from it. The color scale denotes transfer amplitude in the finite Euclidean model; a gravitational interpretation remains provisional.

figures.caption: The first nonzero circle mode converges at second order and remains below the proved dispersion bound.
figures.alt: Circle-mode dispersion error follows a quadratic lattice-spacing bound.
figures.description: Both axes are logarithmic. The measured first-mode dispersion error and its stated quadratic envelope lie nearly together as lattice spacing varies. The displayed finite low-mode comparison illustrates second-order convergence.

figures.caption: The curves show intermediate windows of spectral dimension for a finite cycle and a finite two-dimensional torus. Departures in the ultraviolet and infrared reflect the finite size of the models rather than additional dimensions.
figures.alt: Finite cycle and torus spectral-dimension curves have intermediate plateaus.
figures.description: Spectral dimension is plotted against diffusion time. The cycle curve has an intermediate window near one and the torus curve a window near two, followed by decay at long times. Short- and long-time departures reflect the finite models.

figures.caption: The proof boundary. Finite packet, circuit, leakage, Feshbach, connection, and spectral identities are established here. Constraint closure and the physical continuum claims remain conjectural.
figures.alt: A chart separates finite results from conjectural quantum-spacetime targets.
figures.description: The rows list finite packets, circuits, leakage, Feshbach reduction, connections, spectral tests, and later physical targets. The first group is marked in the proved-here column. Constraint closure and the Lorentzian, Einstein, and spin-two targets are marked conjectural.

figures.caption: The finite mathematical layers developed in the article and the separate limit criteria needed at the continuum boundary.
figures.alt: A sequence of finite quantum layers leading to separate continuum-limit criteria.
figures.description: Boxes progress through seed, symmetry packets, circuit paths, channels, constraints, effective dynamics, Euclidean transfer, and continuum tower. A line groups the finite exact layer separately from the limit criteria at the final stage.

figures.caption: The dimension reached by all local operators is linear in Schmidt rank.
figures.alt: Local orbit dimension increases linearly with Schmidt rank.
figures.description: With the displayed local dimension fixed at four, the plotted orbit dimensions are four, eight, twelve, and sixteen at Schmidt ranks one through four. The connected points illustrate the finite rank formula under the chapter assumptions.

figures.caption: An operator of charge one moves each cyclic packet to the next packet and has no other transfer blocks.
figures.alt: A charge-one operator advances through four cyclic symmetry packets.
figures.description: Four packet nodes P0 through P3 are arranged in a cycle. Arrows labeled with the charge-one operator go to the next packet and return from P3 to P0. The accompanying identity restricts transfer to those allowed blocks.

figures.caption: A circuit block is the coherent sum of its allowed packet paths. Selection rules remove forbidden paths before amplitudes are evaluated.
figures.alt: Allowed packet paths across a four-gate circuit.
figures.description: Columns of three packet nodes represent successive gate stages. Links join permitted transfers between columns, while missing links represent forbidden transfers. A circuit block is obtained by coherently summing its surviving paths.

figures.caption: Exact transition amplitude in a two packet model and the linear commutator bound.
figures.alt: An exact two-packet transition amplitude lies below a commutator envelope.
figures.description: The exact leakage amplitude oscillates over the time interval. The dotted commutator envelope rises linearly and then saturates at one. The exact curve remains below that envelope in the displayed model.

figures.caption: A moving rank one packet on the Bloch sphere. The Kato evolution transports the range without choosing a phase convention for its eigenvector.
figures.alt: A moving rank-one packet traced on the Bloch sphere.
figures.description: A three-dimensional Bloch-sphere coordinate plot shows a curved path near the upper part of the sphere. It illustrates transport of a one-dimensional range. The Kato construction follows that range without choosing an eigenvector phase.

figures.caption: A density matrix or observable carries two packet addresses. Diagonal packets contain populations and internal observables. Off diagonal packets contain coherences.
figures.alt: An operator matrix is divided into diagonal and off-diagonal packet blocks.
figures.description: Rows and columns are grouped into three packet address ranges, producing a three-by-three array of shaded blocks. A block has an output packet address and an input packet address. Diagonal blocks contain within-packet information; off-diagonal blocks contain cross-packet coherence.

figures.caption: Amplitude damping transfers population and contracts the coherence packet.
figures.alt: Amplitude damping changes populations and reduces the coherence magnitude.
figures.description: Six bars compare the two input populations and input coherence magnitude with their three channel outputs. The ground population increases, the excited population decreases, and the coherence magnitude contracts. The bars depict one finite density-matrix example.

figures.caption: The syndrome packets of the three qubit repetition code. Each packet has dimension two and carries the full logical state.
figures.alt: Four two-dimensional syndrome packets of the repetition code.
figures.description: A four-by-four schematic has one marked diagonal square for each error syndrome. Every marked square is labeled dimension two. Distinct syndrome packets are orthogonal and each retains the full logical state.

figures.caption: The zeros of the Feshbach determinant recover the eigenvalues of the full finite Hamiltonian away from the hidden spectrum.
figures.alt: Zeros of an effective Feshbach determinant align with finite eigenvalues.
figures.description: The plot shows the clipped Feshbach determinant as a function of spectral parameter. Vertical reference lines mark full-Hamiltonian eigenvalues, while sharp features occur near the hidden spectrum. The stated correspondence excludes the hidden-spectrum poles.

figures.caption: A finite hidden spectrum produces an oscillatory memory kernel. The retained dynamics therefore depend on the history of the retained state.
figures.alt: Real and imaginary parts of a finite oscillatory memory kernel.
figures.description: Two curves oscillate above and below zero as time increases, one for the real part and one for the imaginary part. The finite hidden spectrum produces memory, so the retained dynamics depend on earlier retained states.

figures.caption: Eigenvalues of a finite reflection positive Gram matrix. Small numerical negative values would signal either roundoff or failure of the transfer assumptions.
figures.alt: Eigenvalues of a finite reflection-positive Gram matrix.
figures.description: A bar chart lists five Gram-matrix eigenvalues with nonnegative displayed heights. The last eigenvalue is the largest. The manuscript separates a finite positivity check from the assumptions needed for a continuum transfer construction.

figures.caption: Finite periodic lattices show an intermediate dimension window. The ultraviolet and infrared limits return to zero because the state space is finite.
figures.alt: Intermediate spectral-dimension windows for finite periodic lattices.
figures.description: The cycle curve approaches a window near one and the two-dimensional torus curve a window near two. Both ultimately decay toward zero at long diffusion times. These finite-window diagnostics are not proofs of a physical continuum dimension.

figures.caption: The closure obstruction lives in a quotient by the constraint span. Physical compression is automatic for self adjoint constraints and cannot replace this quotient.
figures.alt: Constraint commutators are tested in a quotient by the constraint span.
figures.description: Three boxes connect a constraint commutator to the operator-space quotient by the constraint span and then to the closure obstruction. The accompanying note says that compression to the physical kernel cannot replace this closure test for self-adjoint constraints.

figures.caption: A refinement tower carries Hamiltonians, packets, constraints, and transfer data. Each family has its own compatibility defect.
figures.alt: Four refinement levels carry Hamiltonians, packet projectors, and constraints.
figures.description: Four vertically stacked Hilbert-space levels are connected by refinement arrows. Each level lists its Hamiltonian, packet family, and constraints. The tower keeps the corresponding compatibility defects as separate requirements.

figures.caption: The finite identities occupy the first step. Every later step needs a separate convergence or reconstruction theorem.
figures.alt: A staircase lists separate theorems required beyond finite packet identities.
figures.description: Seven steps progress from finite packet identities through compatible refinement, a self-adjoint continuum limit, a reflection-positive Euclidean limit, local Lorentzian field theory, an Einstein infrared criterion, and a positive massless spin-two sector. Each later step requires its own theorem; the diagram does not assert that the chain has been completed.
